name: Lurasidone
route_note: Oral tablets once daily with food (at least 350 kcal).

discovery.note: Developed in Japan as a D2/5-HT2A antagonist with potent 5-HT7 antagonism.

tagline: Low-metabolic-risk antipsychotic approved for schizophrenia and bipolar depression
summary: Lurasidone is a second-generation antipsychotic approved for schizophrenia and for depressive episodes of bipolar I disorder, alone or with lithium or valproate. It has a favourable metabolic profile but must be taken with food and is sensitive to strong CYP3A4 interactions.
mechanism: Lurasidone antagonises D2 and 5-HT2A receptors and has very high affinity for 5-HT7 receptors, where antagonism has been linked to antidepressant and pro-cognitive effects in animal models. It is also a 5-HT1A partial agonist.
It has negligible affinity for histamine H1 and muscarinic receptors, which explains its low sedation, weight gain and anticholinergic burden.
uses: Depressive episodes of bipolar I disorder (monotherapy in ages 10 and over; adjunct to lithium or valproate in adults)

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: Latuda is approved for schizophrenia in October 2010.

history.title: Bipolar depression
history.detail: Lurasidone is approved for bipolar depression as monotherapy and adjunct.

history.title: EU approval
history.detail: Latuda is approved in the EU for schizophrenia.

history.title: Paediatric bipolar depression
history.detail: Approval is extended to children and adolescents aged 10–17 with bipolar depression.

history.title: Generics
history.detail: Generic lurasidone launches in the US in February 2023.

safety.boxed_warning: Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis; not approved for this use. Suicidal thoughts and behaviours with antidepressant use in young people (where approved for depression).

facts: Lurasidone is contraindicated with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (such as ketoconazole) or inducers (such as rifampicin).
